Present Continuous vs. Be Going to in Questions and Negative Sentences
Apart from the simple future with “will,” we can also use the present continuous tense and the future withbe going to in order to talk about future activities.

You use both the present continuous tense and “be going to” to express future actions. However, there are certain differences between the two forms.

We use the present continuous tense when we describe our plans or arrangements for a specific time in the future. These are generally fixed plans with a determined time and place. When making negative sentences and questions, the present continuous for future arrangements has the following structures:

 

Subject + auxiliary verb to be + not + main verb + ing + complement

 

Example:

 

  • That data structure is not using a tree list.

 

 

Auxiliary verb to be + subject + main verb + ing + Complement +?

 

Example:

 

  • Is that data structure using a tree list?

           Yes, it is.

           No, it isn’t.

 

On the other hand, we use “be going to” when we want to express our purpose or decision to do something. However, it does not imply fixed plans or arrangements, it is simply an intention. When making negative sentences and questions, “be going to” has the following structures:

 

Subject + auxiliary verb to be + not + going to + main verb + complement

 

Example:

 

  • Ronald isn’t going to validate data structures today.

 

Auxiliary verb to be + subject + going to + main verb + complement +?

 

Example:

 

  • Is Ronald going to validate data structures today?

           Yes, he is.

           No, he isn’t.

Modal Verbs Can, Could, Have to and Must
We use the modal verbs can and could to express abilities and possibilities. When we want to express obligation we use the modals have to and must.

The modals can and could are useful to express skills and possible actions. We use can in the present and could in the past.

 

Structure:

 

Subject + can/could + main verb in base form + complement

 

Examples:

 

  • You can try many data structures and then apply the one that fits better with your purpose.
  • We could organize those items in a tree line structure.

 

The modal verbs have to and must are used when referring to obligations. However, there are certain differences to consider.

 

We use must to express a strong obligation that is related to a personal belief or circumstance. It implies certain agreement from the speaker.

 

Structure:

 

Subject + must + main verb in base form + complement

 

Example:

 

  • We must know first each type of data structure before making a decision.

 

We use have to in order to talk about a strong obligation that is related to external circumstances. The speaker doesn’t necessarily agree with the obligation.

 

 

Structure:

 

Subject + have to/ has to + main verb in base form + complement

 

Examples:

 

  • In a tree structure, each list has to operate through a root element.
  • We have to organize the company’s data in an easier manner.

images.text:
Francine: Hello, Laura. Are you organizing the conference for this afternoon? I heard it's going to be very interesting.
Laura: Yes, you must come before 2 pm to get a seat. We are covering very important topics related to database management.
Francine: Unfortunately, I can't go. I have to take my daughter to the dentist. I couldn't reschedule her appointment. Are you talking about data mining?
Laura: No, we aren't focusing on that issue today, but we're discussing data structures.
Francine: That's too bad! I am not going to be able to solve some doubts I have. Can you briefly tell me what data structures are?
Laura: Sure! As you must know, a data structure is the easiest way to organize data on your computer. Its principal components are a series of elementary data types, a system to transfer these data, and particular strategies to manipulate them.

Francine: Could you explain to me how data structures work?
Laura: They work through arrays, which don't have internal links that join their elements because all data have to belong to the same category. On the other hand, they also work through types of lists, which have more than one pointer to join elements. These types of lists can have different functions, such as tree lists. A tree list starts with a root element or an element that doesn't have a predecessor. In this way, the next elements will only have one predecessor. This is an advantage since the process to execute systematic operations becomes faster.

Francine: That's an interesting explanation! I'm not going to forget it. What else are you going to discuss about data structures?
Laura: Well, we have to discuss many important aspects; however, I am not going to mention all of them, only the most common key features. There's another type of list called queue, this one retrieves data in a “first in, first out” structure. For example, when there are tasks that have to wait their turn for execution. Finally, we find the stack lists, in this case, you can only access them at the top, so when you need to insert a new item you're going to remove the last inserted item. In other words, this is a “last in, first out” logic when organizing and retrieving elements.
